choices.text: The browser runs it once, when the class is first defined
choices.why: That is what Node did with `@Labelled` after `tsc`. The CLI does the reading before the browser is involved.

choices.text: The compiler reads it at build time; the browser never sees it
choices.why: Right. Ahead-of-time compilation turns each template into JavaScript that creates the DOM directly.

choices.text: Node strips it like a type annotation and the class runs without it
choices.why: Node's type stripping refused the decorator with a `SyntaxError`; it does not remove syntax.

choices.text: It becomes a call to `new` that the template makes
choices.why: Angular builds the instance; no template calls `new`.

prompt: Which of these belong in the `imports` list of a standalone component's decorator? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a component its template writes as an element
choices.why: Right. That is the case `NG8001` complains about when it is missing.

choices.text: a service the class uses in a method
choices.why: The class's own code needs only the TypeScript `import` line.

choices.text: a pipe its template uses after a `|`
choices.why: Right. Pipes reach the template through this list.

choices.text: a helper function called from the constructor
choices.why: Again the class's code, not the template's; the decorator's list is only for the template.

choices.text: an NgModule like `FormsModule`, for `ngModel`
choices.why: Right. A module brings everything it exports at once.

prompt: In the tidy version of `~/legacy`'s `main.ts`, `BrowserModule` drops out of the providers entirely. Why can it?

choices.text: `bootstrapApplication` sets up everything it provided
choices.why: Right. Starting without a module already does the browser module's job.

choices.text: `provideRouter(routes)` provides everything `BrowserModule` did
choices.why: The router function sets up the router and nothing else.

choices.text: A standalone application cannot import an NgModule at all
choices.why: It can; a standalone component may put a module in its `imports`.

prompt: `week` is a signal created with `equal: (a, b) => a.start === b.start && a.end === b.end`. It is set to a new object with the same two dates. What happens?

choices.text: The signal throws, since its value must not be replaced
choices.why: A signal's value is meant to be replaced; that is what `set` is for.

choices.text: It is not a change, and nothing that reads `week` is disturbed
choices.why: Right. The comparison the signal uses is the one it was given.

choices.text: Every computed reading it runs again at once
choices.why: Even on a real change, a computed waits for its next read.

choices.text: `showDone` and `planned`

prompt: A server sets an `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie. What does `HttpClient` do with it, without any interceptor of yours?

choices.why: The token travels in a header, not in the body.

choices.text: Deletes it, since cookies are a security risk
choices.why: It relies on the cookie; it does not delete it.

choices.text: Copies it into an `Authorization: Bearer` header
choices.why: That header is the job of an interceptor you write, for a signed-in user's token.

choices.text: Copies it into an `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header
choices.why: Right. On every request that changes something. The server checks that the two match, and another site cannot read the cookie to forge the header.
